title: Add representation-aware rendering to formatters

title: Add Representation enum for variable file compression
description:
Add simplified Representation enum (4 levels, not 5):

```rust
enum Representation {
    NameOnly,    // tree entry only
    Structure,   // signatures/headings  
    Snippet,     // first N lines
    Full,        // complete content
}
```

Drop Metadata level - agents don't need file stats.

Add to FileEntry in src/scanner/entry.rs.
Update formatters to use representation levels.

comments.author: Raymond Weitekamp
comments.text:
## Analysis: ESSENTIAL ✅

The Representation enum is the core architectural insight that distinguishes dirpack from other tools.

**Why it matters:**
Current implementation treats all files equally within a phase - every code file either gets signatures or doesn't. But main.rs getting full content is MORE valuable than 10 test files getting signatures.

**Suggested simplification:**
Consider reducing from 5 levels to 4:

```rust
enum Representation {
    NameOnly,    // tree entry only
    Structure,   // signatures/headings  
    Snippet,     // first N lines
    Full,        // complete content
}
```

Rationale: 'Metadata' (size, type) is rarely useful for agents. They want code structure, not file stats.

**Implementation note:**
This is a small code change (add field to FileEntry) but enables the entire mesh decimation architecture. Low effort, high leverage.

comments.author: Raymond Weitekamp

title: Add representation-aware rendering to formatters
description:
Update pipe, full, and json formatters to render files based on their Representation level:

- NameOnly: just filename in tree
- Metadata: filename + size/type
- Structure: filename + signatures
- Snippet: filename + first N lines
- Full: filename + complete content

Each formatter should handle all representation levels.
notes: Merged into dirpack-78h per agent feedback

comments.author: Raymond Weitekamp
comments.text:
## Analysis: NICE TO HAVE (but follows naturally) 🔶

This is a required follow-on to dirpack-78h, not a separate design decision.

**What's already working:**
- Pipe formatter handles signatures well
- Full formatter has structure
- JSON has the right schema

**What needs to change:**
Once files have a Representation field, formatters just need to check it:

```rust
match entry.representation {
    NameOnly => emit_name_only(),
    Structure => emit_with_signatures(),
    Snippet => emit_with_preview(),
    Full => emit_complete(),
}
```

**Not over-engineering because:**
This is just a switch statement, not new architecture. The complexity is in dirpack-78h and dirpack-hnk.

**Suggestion:** 
Merge this into dirpack-78h as 'add Representation enum AND update formatters'. They're not separable - adding the enum without using it in formatters is pointless.

title: Add markdown heading extraction for docs
description:
Currently tree-sitter extracts signatures from code files, but docs (README.md, DESIGN.md) only get line-based snippets.

For Structure representation on markdown files, extract:
- H1/H2/H3 headings as 'signatures'
- First paragraph under each heading as optional context

This would make dirpack output for docs match quality of code output.

Example for README.md at Structure level:
```
README.md:# dirpack,## Features,## Installation,## Quick Start
```

Lower priority than core architecture (78h, hnk) but improves doc handling.

title: Implement greedy budget allocation algorithm
description:
Implement tiered budget allocation (simpler than true greedy):

1. All files start at NameOnly (tree always included)
2. Pass 1: Upgrade top 20% priority files to Structure (use ~40% budget)
3. Pass 2: Upgrade top 10% priority files to Snippet (use ~30% budget)
4. Pass 3: Upgrade top 5% priority files to Full (use remaining budget)

O(n log n) with one sort, vs O(n²) for true greedy.

Key insight: High-priority files should reach higher representation levels before low-priority files advance at all.

comments.author: Raymond Weitekamp
comments.text: Tested current behavior: -t 500 vs -t 2000 yields basically the same ordered stream (tree + signatures) until truncation. There is no per-file upgrade or balanced coverage; output just stops mid-stream when budget is hit. This means we don't get a mesh/decimation effect today. Greedy upgrade allocation would add real value by upgrading files progressively (NameOnly -> Structure -> Snippet -> Full) and spreading budget across more files. Not over-engineering if the goal is graceful degradation; you can keep it minimal with 2-3 levels and a simple upgrade loop.

comments.author: Raymond Weitekamp
comments.text:
## Analysis: ESSENTIAL but SIMPLIFY ✅

The greedy algorithm IS worth the complexity - it produces better output quality per token.

**Current problem:**
Phase-based approach (signatures for ALL code files, then snippets for ALL docs) can waste budget on low-priority files before high-priority ones get full treatment.

**Proposed simplification - Tiered Allocation:**
Instead of true greedy (recalculate after every upgrade), use passes:

1. All files start at NameOnly (tree always included)
2. Pass 1: Upgrade top 20% of files to Structure (use 40% budget)
3. Pass 2: Upgrade top 10% of files to Snippet (use 30% budget)  
4. Pass 3: Upgrade top 5% of files to Full (remaining 30% budget)

This is 80% of the benefit with 20% of the complexity. True greedy would be O(n²) recalculating scores; tiered is O(n log n) with one sort.

**The key insight to preserve:**
High-priority files should reach higher representation levels before low-priority files advance at all. This is the 'mesh decimation' principle.

comments.author: Raymond Weitekamp
comments.text:
## SPACE_FILLING.md Analysis: Critical Review

### Q1: Does tiered allocation already achieve coverage?

**PARTIALLY YES.** 

The tree (NameOnly for all files) guarantees coverage of *existence*. Every file appears somewhere. The problem is *detail concentration* - if the top 20% priority files are all in `src/api/`, you get lopsided output: deep API detail, zero test/docs detail.

Current priority scoring (main.rs=140, tests=50, locks=10) helps but doesn't prevent clustering.

### Q2: Is stratified sampling (% per file type) worth it?

**NO as a hard constraint.**

Forcing '15% budget to docs' wastes tokens if docs are trivial. The category-based priority (code=100, docs=90) already soft-stratifies.

**BUT:** A softer version might help - 'ensure at least 1 file per top-level directory gets Structure'. This is minimum coverage without forced waste.

### Q3: Should we add diversity penalty?

**SKEPTICAL.**

If src/api/ IS the most important subsystem, we SHOULD detail it heavily. A diversity penalty forces including less-valuable files just for spread.

**Exception case:** If we're upgrading 10 files in src/api/ to Structure and 0 files elsewhere, that's probably wrong. A per-directory cap (max 5 files at Snippet/Full per dir) would help without complex penalty math.

### Q4: Hybrid (skeleton → upgrades) vs pure tiered?

**Already hybrid.** Current plan = skeleton (tree) + upgrades (tiered allocation). The 'decimate if tight' step is premature optimization for edge cases.

---

## Recommendation: ADD PER-DIRECTORY CAP

The simplest change that adds coverage guarantees:

```rust
const MAX_DETAIL_PER_DIR: usize = 5;

// In upgrade loop:
if upgrades_in_dir[dir] >= MAX_DETAIL_PER_DIR {
    skip_to_next_candidate();
}
```

This prevents 'lopsided' results without:
- Complex stratification rules
- Diversity penalty calculations  
- Space-filling curve overhead

**Should this be a separate issue or part of dirpack-hnk?**
I'd add it to hnk as an implementation detail, not a new issue. It's a 5-line guard clause.

comments.author: Raymond Weitekamp
comments.text: Coverage analysis: ran . Output includes a full tree with many dirs (docs/, dspy/, tests/, .github/, etc.), so baseline coverage exists, but detail is lopsided: we dump a big tree + a prioritized prefix of signatures until truncation, and budget even overshot (2760/2000). There’s no per-file upgrade balancing across dirs. So tiered allocation alone won’t guarantee balanced detail; space-filling/diversity would add value if we want even coverage of detailed info.

comments.author: Raymond Weitekamp
comments.text:
## What NOT to add (over-engineering risks):

### ❌ Hilbert/Z-order curves
Files aren't points in 2D space. Directory hierarchy already provides locality. Converting to 'feature space' then applying space-filling curves adds complexity with unclear benefit.

### ❌ Hard stratified budgets  
Forcing '40% to code, 15% to docs' assumes we know the right ratios. We don't. Let priority scoring handle relative importance.

### ❌ Blue-noise / Poisson-disc sampling
Cool for graphics, overkill here. Per-directory cap achieves similar diversity with 5 lines of code vs. distance calculations in abstract feature space.

### ❌ Three-phase hybrid (skeleton → upgrades → decimate)
Two phases (skeleton + upgrades) is enough. 'Decimate if tight' handles edge cases that rarely occur in practice (budget < tree size).

---

**Keep it simple:** Tiered allocation + per-directory cap. That's the 80/20 solution.

comments.author: Raymond Weitekamp
comments.text: Coverage analysis follow-up: ran cargo run -- pack ~/Documents/GitHub/dspy -t 2000 -v. Output includes a very broad tree (docs/, dspy/, tests/, .github/, etc.), but detailed content is still lopsided because we emit the tree + a prioritized prefix of signatures until truncation. Budget even overshot (2760/2000). So tiered allocation alone doesn’t ensure balanced detail; diversity/space-filling would help.

comments.author: Raymond Weitekamp
comments.text:
## Final verdict on space-filling:

**Add to dirpack-hnk:** Per-directory cap (MAX_DETAIL_PER_DIR = 5)

**Do NOT create new issues for:**
- Stratified sampling
- Diversity penalties
- Space-filling curves
- Minimum coverage guarantees

**Rationale:** Priority scoring already distributes across directories (README in root, Cargo.toml in root, main.rs in src/, etc.). The per-directory cap is defensive insurance, not the primary mechanism.

If coverage becomes a real problem in testing, we can revisit. But let's ship the simple version first.

title: Add coverage-aware upgrade selection (space-filling)
description: Optional enhancement: add diversity/coverage heuristics to upgrade selection (e.g., per-directory quotas, stratified sampling, or diversity penalty on similar paths) so detailed representations aren’t lopsided after the tree baseline. Informed by SPACE_FILLING.md.

title: Handle hidden directories as NameOnly
description:
Hidden directories (.git/, .claude/, .beads/) should:
- Always appear in tree (NameOnly representation)
- Never descend into contents
- Never extract signatures

Add special handling in scanner and packer modules.

comments.author: Raymond Weitekamp
comments.text:
## Analysis: NICE TO HAVE 🔶

This is valuable but not as critical as the core architecture (78h + hnk).

**Current behavior:**
Hidden dirs fully excluded when include_hidden=false. Agent never knows .claude/ or .beads/ exist.

**Proposed behavior:**
Show hidden dirs in tree (NameOnly) but don't descend. Agent sees the directory exists, can ask for more if needed.

**Why it's nice but not essential:**
- Agents rarely need hidden dir contents
- If they do, user can run dirpack with include_hidden=true
- The 'topology preserving' benefit is modest

**Implementation is simple:**
In scanner/walk.rs, detect hidden dirs and emit as NameOnly entries without recursing.

**Suggestion:**
Do this AFTER the core architecture lands. It's a 10-line change that doesn't block anything else.

title: Build eval harness for allocation algorithms
description: Create automated eval metrics to measure allocation quality before/after mesh decimation changes. Metrics: budget accuracy, coverage spread, lopsidedness, signature density, path diversity, entry point coverage.

comments.author: Raymond Weitekamp
comments.text:
## Metric Critique

### Tier 1 - Good but needs refinement:

**Budget accuracy (<10%)** - ESSENTIAL. But measure UNDER-budget separately from over-budget. Under-budget by 8% is fine (leaving headroom). Over-budget by 2% is a bug.

**Coverage spread** - GOOD metric. But "top-level dirs" might be too coarse. For monorepos, depth=2 coverage matters more (e.g., packages/foo, packages/bar).

**Lopsidedness** - USEFUL but the formula is noisy. Better: Gini coefficient of files-at-detail-level per directory. Or simpler: count of dirs with >5 detailed files (should be 0-1).

**Graceful degradation** - CRITICAL. Also add: at 500 tokens, should still have tree + ≥3 signatures. Don't collapse to "just the tree" too early.

### Tier 2 - Mixed:

**Signature density** - GOOD proxy for "did we extract useful code info". But normalize by language - Python files have fewer explicit signatures than Rust.

**Path diversity** - GOOD. Equivalent to coverage spread at depth=2.

**Entry point coverage** - ESSENTIAL. Binary: did we include main/index/lib at Structure+ level? This should be 100% at all budgets >500 tokens.

### Missing metrics:

1. **Config file coverage** - Cargo.toml/package.json/pyproject.toml should always be included at Metadata+ level
2. **README inclusion** - At budgets >1K, README should have at least first 3 lines
3. **Signature/tree ratio** - If tree takes >40% of budget, we're wasting tokens on structure vs content
4. **Parse success rate** - What % of code files got tree-sitter signatures vs fell back to nothing?

comments.author: Raymond Weitekamp
comments.text:
## Implementation Decision

**Recommendation: cargo test + optional 'dirpack eval' subcommand**

### Why both:

1. **cargo test** (Tier 1 metrics) - Run on every build. Fast assertions:
   - Budget accuracy assertion: actual <= target * 1.02
   - Entry point assertion: main/lib/index always at Structure+
   - These catch regressions immediately

2. **dirpack eval <path>** subcommand (Tier 2-3) - For manual analysis:
   - JSON output with all metrics
   - Comparison mode: eval --compare before.json after.json
   - Human-readable report

### Test fixtures:
- Small synthetic repo (10 files, known structure)
- Medium realistic repo snapshot (subset of DSPy)
- Config-only edge case (just package.json + README)

Don't download external repos in CI. Commit small fixtures.

comments.author: Raymond Weitekamp
comments.text:
## Baseline Results - CRITICAL FINDINGS

### DSPy (large Python project)
| Budget | Chars | Dirs | Sigs |
|--------|-------|------|------|
| 500    | 11119 | 5    | 0    |
| 1000   | 11119 | 5    | 0    |
| 2000   | 11119 | 5    | 0    |
| 4000   | 16319 | 5    | 37   |
| 8000   | 32702 | 5    | 152  |

### build123d (Python CAD library)
| Budget | Chars | Dirs | Sigs |
|--------|-------|------|------|
| 500    | 12532 | 6    | 0    |
| 1000   | 12532 | 6    | 0    |
| 2000   | 12532 | 6    | 0    |
| 4000   | 16230 | 6    | 35   |
| 8000   | 32785 | 6    | 191  |

### Problems Found

1. **NO GRACEFUL DEGRADATION** - Same output at 500/1000/2000 tokens. Spine alone is ~11K chars (~2750 tokens).

2. **Budget not respected** - At 500 token budget, outputting 2750+ tokens. Spine ignores budget.

3. **Signatures only at 4K+** - Tree consumes all budget below 4K.

### Root Cause
Spine phase outputs everything regardless of budget. Need sub-budget for spine (max 40%).

comments.author: Raymond Weitekamp
comments.text:
## Consensus Response: Eval Harness Design

### Agreement on Metric Refinements

**Budget accuracy** - AGREE with asymmetric treatment. Proposed thresholds:
- Over-budget: FAIL if actual > target * 1.02 (2% tolerance)
- Under-budget: WARN if actual < target * 0.70 (wasting 30%+ budget)

**Coverage spread at depth=2** - AGREE. Better than top-level for monorepos.

**Lopsidedness simplification** - AGREE with 'dirs with >5 detailed files' metric. Simpler than Gini, actionable.

**Signature/tree ratio** - AGREE this is key. Proposed threshold: tree_tokens / total_tokens <= 0.40

### Agreed Implementation Approach

**cargo test + dirpack eval** - YES, this is the right split.

cargo test assertions (hard failures):
- Budget overshoot: actual <= target * 1.02
- Entry points: main/lib/index at Structure+ when budget >= 500
- Config files: Cargo.toml/package.json/pyproject.toml present when budget >= 300

dirpack eval (analysis):
- JSON output with all Tier 1+2 metrics
- --compare mode for before/after
- --threshold flag to set pass/fail levels

### Proposed Thresholds Summary

| Metric | Pass | Warn | Fail |
|--------|------|------|------|
| Budget overshoot | ≤2% | n/a | >2% |
| Budget undershoot | ≥70% | 50-70% | <50% |
| Tree ratio | ≤40% | 40-50% | >50% |
| Entry point coverage | 100% | n/a | <100% |
| Config coverage | 100% | n/a | <100% |
| Lopsided dirs (>5 files) | 0-1 | 2 | >2 |

### Open Question

Should we fix the spine budget bug FIRST (as a separate issue) before building the full eval harness? Current baseline shows spine ignores budget entirely - that's a bug, not a feature gap.

comments.author: Raymond Weitekamp
comments.text:
VOTE: AGREE - Fix spine bug first.

**Reasoning:**
1. Eval harness measures allocation QUALITY (coverage, lopsidedness, diversity). But we can't measure quality if basic budget CONSTRAINT is broken.

2. TDD argument doesn't apply here - this isn't 'write failing test then fix'. The test is trivial: 'output <= budget'. No harness needed for that.

3. Spine fix is small scope - add budget check in spine.rs, truncate/collapse when tight. Probably 20-30 lines.

4. Once spine respects budget, THEN we can measure quality metrics meaningfully.

**Proposed new issue:**
- Title: 'Fix spine phase to respect budget constraint'
- Priority: P0
- Blocks: dirpack-wuf (eval harness)
- Estimate: Small (spine.rs only)

**Acceptance criteria:**
- At 500 token budget, output ≤ 520 tokens (2% tolerance)
- At 1000 token budget, output ≤ 1020 tokens
- Tree should truncate/collapse, not just overflow

comments.author: Raymond Weitekamp
comments.text: Analysis: Metrics are directionally right, but need tweaks. Budget accuracy must use same estimator as packer and enforce truncation; current output can exceed target because tree is not budget-limited. Coverage spread should derive top-level dirs from file paths (git scan does not emit directory entries, so coverage is N/A). Lopsidedness should be N/A when no detailed files; consider entropy/Gini as a more stable indicator. Signature density is noisy across languages; normalize by code-only tokens or count unique signatures per detailed file. Entry-point coverage should be repo-specific (Cargo.toml/pyproject.toml/package.json + main/lib/index). Add a metric for "tree-only dominates budget" to catch overshoot. Baseline (current dirpack on dspy): tokens=2779 for target 500/1000/2000 (accuracy +456%/+178%/+39%), sig_files=0, coverage N/A, lopsided N/A. At target 4000: tokens=4079 (+2%), sig_files=12, lopsided=1.5. This shows no graceful degradation for low budgets and budget overshoot before any detailed coverage.

comments.author: Raymond Weitekamp
comments.text:
Agree with Claude’s refinements: compute coverage from file paths (git scan lacks dirs), align budget accuracy with packer token estimator + enforce truncation, and treat lopsidedness/coverage as N/A when no detailed files. Also add an overshoot metric (tree-only > target) to catch current failure mode.

Approach: I’d avoid running evals via cargo test by default; keep unit tests for metric functions in cargo test, and put integration evals in a dirpack eval subcommand (or scripts/eval.py) that CI can invoke explicitly. If we want both, gate evals behind a feature flag or an ignored test.

Proposed initial thresholds (tunable after baseline):
- Budget accuracy: <=10% for targets >=1000; <=20% for 500 (tighten later).
- Coverage spread: >=0.6 at 1000, >=0.75 at 2000, >=0.85 at 4000 (repos with >=4 top-level dirs).
- Lopsidedness (max/mean detailed files per top dir): <=2.5 at 1000, <=2.0 at 2000, <=1.5 at 4000.
- Graceful degradation: monotonic nondecreasing coverage/path_diversity/sig_files as budget increases; error should not worsen.
- Signature density: measure + report for now; avoid hard threshold until we see baseline variability.

No objections to a dirpack eval subcommand; I would not fail cargo test on external repo evals.

comments.author: Raymond Weitekamp
comments.text: VOTE: AGREE - spine currently ignores budget so low-budget runs overshoot massively and will fail evals. We should fix budget enforcement in spine (or at least add truncation/partial tree) before locking eval harness thresholds; otherwise tests will be red by construction and not diagnostic. P0 bug fix before eval harness makes sense.

comments.author: Raymond Weitekamp
comments.text:
## Eval Harness Complete

### Artifacts Created
- `scripts/eval.sh` - Main eval harness (JSON output)
- `scripts/eval-summary.sh` - Summary report generator
- `tests/fixtures/small_project/` - Test fixture (7 files)
- `baselines/` - Captured baseline measurements

### Baseline Results Summary

**Small Project (7 files)**: PASS at all budgets
- Tree ratio: 33% (good)
- Signatures: 18 at all levels
- Entry points: main.rs, lib.rs, Cargo.toml all present

**DSPy (large Python project)**: FAIL at 500-2000 tokens
- 500 tokens: 455% overshoot, 0 signatures, 100% tree
- 4000 tokens: 2% overshoot, 38 signatures, 69% tree (first passing)

**build123d (large Python project)**: FAIL at 500-2000 tokens
- 500 tokens: 526% overshoot, 0 signatures, 100% tree
- 16000 tokens: 1.8% overshoot, 609 signatures (first clean pass)

### Documented Thresholds

| Metric | PASS | WARN | FAIL |
|--------|------|------|------|
| Budget overshoot | ≤2% | - | >2% |
| Tree ratio | ≤40% | 40-50% | >50% |
| Entry points (≥500tok) | 100% | - | <100% |

### Root Cause Confirmed
Spine phase ignores budget entirely. For large projects, spine alone exceeds typical budgets (2700+ tokens for DSPy/build123d).

### Next Step
Fix spine budget constraint (separate P0 issue). Re-run eval to verify improvement.
